query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, increasing the Al content beyond a baseline (e.g., Al0.1) raises the atomic size misfit, which in turn strengthens chemical short-range order (SRO). This synergistic effect of enhanced lattice strain and SRO destabilizes the single‐phase structure, causing a controlled onset of multiphase behavior (e.g., formation of fcc and bcc mixtures) that correlates with a deterioration in multifunctional properties such as high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA in its typical multiphase state, with the baseline composition being Al0.1 that exhibits a stable single-phase configuration.
generation.intervention: Systematically increase the Al content (thereby increasing the atomic size misfit) while maintaining identical heat-treatment conditions designed to control the level of chemical short-range order.
generation.conditions: Samples will be processed under controlled thermal histories and compared under multiple regimes including high-temperature exposure, radiation environments, and cryogenic testing. The baseline for comparison is the known single-phase behavior of the Al0.1 composition.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical short-range order (SRO) along with lattice strain induced by atomic size misfit.
generation.mechanism: A higher Al content increases the atomic size misfit in the alloy, which intensifies lattice strain. This increased strain promotes the formation of chemical SRO. The combined effect of misfit-induced strain and enhanced SRO reaches a threshold where the originally stable single-phase (Al0.1) decomposes into multiphase structures (e.g., a mixture of fcc and bcc phases) leading to the emergence of precipitates, with a concomitant loss of the desirable multifunctional properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Al contents above a critical threshold (e.g., >0.3–0.5 mole fraction) will exhibit a clear transition from a single-phase microstructure to multiphase behavior with detectable precipitates. This microstructural evolution will be accompanied by measurable reductions in high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, environmental resistance, and cryogenic toughness relative to the Al0.1 baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: The Al0.1 CrCoFeNi alloy, which has been previously observed to maintain a stable single-phase structure with optimal multifunctional properties.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable within the composition window where Al is varied (approximately 0.1 to 2 mole fractions) under controlled thermal and processing conditions. Its predictive capability may not extend to systems where other alloying elements or processing variables deviate significantly from those assumed.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative threshold of the Al content that triggers the phase transition, and the full extent of the interplay between lattice strain and SRO, may depend on subtle variations in processing history and microstructural factors not fully captured in the current framework.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy samples with Al content varying systematically from the baseline value (e.g., Al0.1) up to higher mole fractions (e.g., 0.5 to 2.0) under identical heat-treatment conditions to ensure comparable chemical short-range order. Subject the samples to phase identification (using XRD and TEM), microstructural analysis (using atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM to probe SRO), and functional property testing (including mechanical tests at high and cryogenic temperatures along with radiation exposure assessments).
measurements: Phase composition and quantification via X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy
Characterization of local chemical order using atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM
Mechanical property measurements (e.g., hardness, yield strength, ductility) across temperature regimes
Performance tests under simulated radiation exposure conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the Al content does not lead to a systematic onset of multiphase behavior (or precipitate formation) and no correlated degradation in high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, environmental resistance, or cryogenic toughness is observed compared to the Al0.1 baseline—despite clear evidence of increased lattice strain and SRO—then the mechanistic link proposed by the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. Here, an unexpected ductile–brittle–ductile transition is discovered in a multiphase high‐entropy alloy (HEA) aged in an intermediate temperature regime. Unlike the classical thermal embrittlement driven by grain boundary effects, this transition originates from the dynamic evolution of local chemical order (LCO) and phase boundary (PB) configurations in HEAs. Aging within the embrittlement‐prone regime enhances chemical ordering, increases the density of ordered domains, and induces jagged PBs, collectively triggering plastic instability and the ductile−to−brittle transition. In contrast, aging outside this regime suppresses excessive ordering and promotes the formation of ductile interphase transition zones, facilitating a brittle−to−ductile recovery. The findings offer new insights into the thermal behavior of HEAs and challenge the established paradigm of thermal embrittlement. decision.trend: Early investigations in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys have mostly relied on empirical correlations and compositional tuning (e.g., varying the Al content) to observe changes in phase structure and precipitation behavior under irradiation or mechanical testing. In PMC4999872, alloys with near-zero Al (Al0.1) were single phase and stable under hostile conditions, whereas increased Al content led to multiphase behavior with distinct coherent precipitates. These studies typically isolated either the effect of lattice strain (from atomic size misfit) or chemical ordering (short-range order) on phase stability. However, despite these successes, the direct mechanistic linkage between atomic-level interactions (both lattice strain and chemical short-range order) and the multifunctional performance criteria (high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, robustness at cryogenic temperatures, and environmental resistance) remains unresolved.
decision.unsolved: The key gap is a unified, testable mechanistic hypothesis that quantitatively connects changes in atomic size misfit and chemical short-range order to phase stability. Particularly, it remains unclear how a controlled variation (against a well‐established baseline) in parameters like Al content—affecting both lattice strain and ordering kinetics—directly dictates the onset of multiphase behavior and correlates with the retention of desirable multifunctional properties.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the Al content (and hence the atomic size misfit) in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys while controlling heat-treatment conditions to moderate chemical short-range order. Use a well‐established baseline (e.g., the Al0.1 single-phase alloy) as a reference to compare phase stability and precipitation kinetics.
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the trend seen in PMC4999872, where increasing Al content led to multiphase behavior. By methodically adjusting the compositional parameter that governs lattice strain and, concurrently, the conditions that affect chemical ordering, the experiment will test whether a combined effect of misfit-induced lattice strain and chemical short-range order controls phase stability. Observation of a threshold behavior in phase transformations or precipitate formation—relative to the baseline—would support the unified mechanistic hypothesis, while a lack of such correlation would serve as falsification.
